target.title: Lipper: Synthesizing Thy Speech using Multi-View Lipreading
target.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 33 (AAAI-19), pp. 2588-2595

read.pdf: Fig. 1–3 captions and Tables 1–12 as represented in text.txt

entries.text: Lipper frames lipreading as regression from silent video to reconstructed speech rather than fixed-vocabulary phrase classification.
entries.condition: The paper's proposed task and system; no language or phrase classifier is used for speech reconstruction.
entries.quote:
It does this by mod-
eling lipreading as a regression rather than a classiﬁcation
task.

entries.text: The authors claim that combining silent video views improves speech reconstruction over single-view results.
entries.condition: Multi-view speech reconstruction; detailed evidence is in speaker-dependent PESQ tables.

entries.text: The authors describe Lipper as language- and vocabulary-independent because mapping lip movements to speech does not use word or sentence mappings.
entries.condition: The claim is made for the reconstruction model; the paper's fixed-phrase OuluVS2 experiments and demos do not constitute broad language testing.

entries.text: Lipper is presented as near real-time because it can start producing audio after detecting lip movement, without waiting for the complete sentence.
entries.condition: Use-time claim; the quantitative comparison is Table 11, with timing details incompletely specified.

entries.text: Lipper produces decoded audio and associated text; the text branch classifies encoded reconstructed audio into predefined categories.
entries.condition: Audio is decoded from the reconstruction network output; text is produced by a separate classifier over encoded audio.

entries.text: OuluVS2 contains 53 speakers, 10 phrases, and five concurrent camera views at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.
entries.condition: OuluVS2 audiovisual dataset used for reconstruction; the dataset section says the cameras record simultaneously.

entries.text: The view classifier labels images as one of five discrete poses: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, or 90°.
entries.condition: Image-level view classification; training and test classes are reported as uniformly represented.

entries.text: The view classifier uses ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 features, a 1,024-unit dense layer, and a five-unit softmax output.
entries.condition: Transfer-learned view classifier; cross-entropy objective.

entries.text: The view classifier is trained on 224×224 lip-region images with batch size 100 for 30 epochs using Adam.
entries.condition: View-classifier training; the paper does not identify the train/test image split.

entries.text: View-classifier training and testing use equal numbers of samples from each pose class.
entries.condition: Balanced class distribution; sample counts and partition protocol are not provided.

entries.text: The view classifier's reported overall accuracy is 96.7% on its balanced five-pose classification task.
entries.condition: View-classifier test data; equal class representation is stated, but the test split and speaker composition are not.

entries.text: Speech reconstruction uses 128×128 lip-region images and predicts LPC+LSP-encoded audio with a 50-unit output layer.
entries.condition: STCNN+BiGRU speech-reconstruction model.

entries.text: The video model is STCNN+BiGRU; audio is represented with LPC order 24 and LSP encoding.
entries.condition: Audio sampled at 20,000 Hz before LPC encoding; LSP represents LPC coefficients.
entries.quote:
LPC order was
found out to be optimal at 24.

entries.text: The reconstruction network is described as seven STCNN layers, two BiGRU layers, and a 50-unit output; listed STCNN widths are 32, 32, 64, 64, 128, and 128, and BiGRU widths are 64 and 32.
entries.value: 7 STCNN layers (listed widths 32, 32, 64, 64, 128, 128); 2 BiGRU layers (64, 32); output 50
entries.condition: Architecture description in the paper; the stated number of STCNN layers and listed widths do not match in count.

entries.text: The reconstruction model is trained for 60 epochs and fine-tuned for 20 epochs.
entries.condition: Speech-reconstruction network; optimizer, learning rate, and checkpoint rule are not stated in this passage.

entries.text: Training audio is sampled at 20,000 Hz, encoded with LPC order 24, and paired with image sequences in five-step timesteps.
entries.condition: Speech-reconstruction training input.

entries.text: For speaker-dependent experiments, the authors say each speaker's data were split into two training phrases and one test phrase from a three-phrase set.
entries.value: 2 train phrases; 1 test phrase; 3 phrases in stated split
entries.condition: Same speaker occurs in training and test; the exact phrases and how this three-phrase subset relates to the ten-phrase dataset are not explained.

entries.text: Speaker-independent training uses all but two speakers and tests on the two held-out speakers.
entries.condition: All phrases from training speakers are used; held-out test speakers are later identified as speakers 38 and 39.
entries.quote:
The model then was trained on all but two speakers for all
their phrases.

entries.text: OOV evaluation uses ten leave-one-phrase-out training iterations for each speaker, testing on a phrase absent from that iteration's training data.
entries.value: 10 iterations; 1 of 10 phrases held out per iteration
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent OOV evaluation; speaker identity is present in training and test, while phrase identity is held out per round.

entries.text: The text-prediction network has four fully connected layers of sizes 1,000, 500, 100, and 10, with dropout 0.5 after the 500- and 100-unit layers; it uses batch size 10 for 20 epochs.
entries.condition: Classifier takes encoded audio from a pretrained reconstruction model and predicts one of ten phrase classes.

entries.text: Text-prediction Config-1 randomly partitions encoded audios from all speakers into train, test, and validation sets in a 70/10/20 ratio.
entries.condition: Random sample-level split across all speakers; speaker-disjointness is not reported.

entries.text: Text-prediction Config-2 trains on encoded audios from 70% of speakers and divides the remaining speakers' audios between validation (10%) and test (20%).
entries.value: 70% train speakers; remaining 30% divided 10% validation and 20% test
entries.unit: % of speakers as worded in paper
entries.condition: Speaker-partitioned text classifier; percentages are reported as in the paper, without a count of speakers in each subset.

entries.text: Text-prediction Config-1 reports 97.0% accuracy.
entries.condition: Ten-class text prediction from encoded reconstructed audio; random audio-level train/test/validation split 70/10/20 across all speakers.
entries.quote: Accuracy 97.0 78.5 95.6

entries.text: Text-prediction Config-2 reports 78.5% accuracy.
entries.condition: Ten-class text prediction from encoded reconstructed audio; speaker-level split, with 70% of speakers for training and remaining audios divided for validation/test.
entries.quote: Accuracy 97.0 78.5 95.6

entries.text: The paper reports 95.6% as the best accuracy from Petridis et al. (2017) for comparison.
entries.condition: Petridis et al. (2017) multi-view lipreading result on OuluVS2, quoted as the best accuracy reported in that paper; the exact matched evaluation split is not given here.
entries.quote:
We present the best accuracy reported in the paper
by (Petridis et al. 2017) for comparison.

entries.text: The authors say Config-1 exceeds the cited best model but attribute this to Lipper's train-test configuration, making it an acknowledged comparability caveat.
entries.condition: Comparison is between text-prediction accuracies; Config-1 has a random sample split across speakers, unlike Config-2's speaker-level split.
entries.quote:
We believe
this is due to the train-test conﬁguration of Lipper itself.

entries.text: The paper gives 10% as random-guess accuracy for the ten-class text-prediction task.
entries.condition: Uniform random choice among the ten phrase classes.

entries.text: PESQ is the audio-quality metric; the paper describes its score range as −0.5 to 4.5 and says higher scores indicate better quality.
entries.condition: PESQ is described as an ITU-T measure for 3.2 kHz codecs; speech comparisons are aligned before scoring.
entries.quote:
The range
of PESQ varies from -0.5 to 4.5, where speech quality in-
creases with increasing score.

entries.text: Speaker-dependent single-view Lipper PESQ means are 2.002 (0°), 1.750 (30°), 1.642 (45°), 1.744 (60°), and 1.804 (90°).
entries.condition: OuluVS2 speaker-dependent single-view speech reconstruction; two phrases train and one phrase tests per speaker under the stated three-phrase split; mean aggregation details are not given.

entries.text: The comparison row for Ephrat and Peleg (2017) reports single-view PESQ means 1.72, 1.57, 1.48, 1.46, and 1.52 for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.
entries.condition: Prior Vid2Speech result reproduced in Table 4; the target paper does not give matched split or test-condition details for this baseline.

entries.text: The authors claim Lipper's single-view PESQ is better than Ephrat and Peleg (2017) at every tested angle.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent single-view comparison in Table 4; baseline protocol equivalence is not established in the paper.
entries.quote:
our results are better
for all the views than (Ephrat and Peleg 2017)

entries.text: The authors say speaker-dependent models score significantly better than speaker-independent models, attributing the gap to speaker-specific voice features absent from training for held-out identities.
entries.condition: Their speaker-independent results use two held-out speakers; no significance test is described for the word significantly.

entries.text: The authors concede the system does not work very well in speaker-independent settings, calling this a deployment problem.
entries.condition: Speaker-independent evaluation; tested on two held-out speakers.
entries.quote:
the system does not work very
well on them.

entries.text: The authors observe that the male test result is better and hypothesize that the dataset's male majority biases voice generation toward male voices.
entries.condition: Speaker-independent test with one male and one female speaker; the explanation is explicitly presented as the authors' belief.
entries.quote:
we believe this is so since the number of male
speakers in the dataset are in a majority thus forming a bias
for Lipper in favour of male voice generation.

entries.text: Audio-only user study: reconstructed speech from 25 speakers was presented to 10 annotators, with four choices per item (one correct and three random options from ten classes); annotators could replay audio freely.
entries.value: 25 speakers; 10 annotators; 4 options; 1 correct + 3 random; 10 classes
entries.condition: Audio-only phrase identification; number of judgments per annotator and total trials are not stated.
entries.quote:
In the ﬁrst study, we gave reconstructed speech of 25
speakers to 10 different annotators

entries.text: Audio-visual user study showed speaker video with reconstructed audio and asked annotators to choose among ten phrase classes.
entries.condition: Audio-visual identification; annotator count, participant demographics, total trials, and randomization are not specified for this condition.
entries.quote:
Then, the annotators were asked to
choose among 10 phrase classes for the audio-video se-
quence that they just listened to.

entries.text: Audio-only study accuracy is 80.25%, with reported annotator-accuracy variance 2.72%.
entries.condition: Audio-only four-choice protocol: one correct plus three random options; 25 speakers and 10 annotators; annotators could replay.
entries.quote: Audio-only 80.25 2.72

entries.text: Audio-visual study accuracy is 81.25%, with reported inter-annotator accuracy variance 1.97%.
entries.condition: Video-plus-reconstructed-audio phrase identification among ten classes; paper does not report total trials or participant details.
entries.quote: Audio-visual 81.25 1.97

entries.text: The paper gives 25% as chance accuracy for the four-option audio-only study and 10% for the ten-class audio-visual study.
entries.condition: Audio-only four alternatives; audio-visual ten phrase classes.
entries.quote:
In the audio-only study, a dice throw could get 25% of the
annotations right

entries.text: The authors caution that PESQ did not always track perceived quality: some noisy audios scored highly and some clearer audios scored poorly.
entries.condition: Motivates the supplementary user study; no threshold or reliability analysis is reported.
entries.quote: not always perfect.

entries.text: The authors conclude that reconstructed audio has significant intelligibility, supported by their two phrase-identification studies.
entries.condition: User-study results; accuracy is reported without confidence intervals or inferential tests.

entries.text: The authors use demo videos of non-dataset speakers speaking Hindi, English, and Chinese as qualitative evidence for language and vocabulary independence; they train speaker-dependent models for these demonstrations.
entries.condition: Qualitative demonstration only; no quantitative non-dataset-language benchmark or held-out language protocol is reported.
entries.quote:
The non-dataset speakers and the
languages they speak show the language and vocabulary
independence of the model.

entries.text: The authors concede that generated audios can be robotic and lack emotion, prosody, or modulation because the model uses only lip-region input, not nose, throat, or tongue cues.
entries.condition: Speech quality limitation of the lip-only sensing approach.

entries.text: The authors concede that Lipper currently requires a controlled setting with little speaker movement and a stable angle toward the camera.
entries.condition: Deployment limitation; changing poses and movement are identified as future work.

entries.text: The paper concludes Lipper is real-time, language/vocabulary-independent, multi-view, and speaker-independent, although its own deployment discussion says speaker-independent performance remains weak.
entries.condition: Conclusion-level characterization; qualify speaker independence with the reported two-speaker evaluation and limitation.
entries.quote:
In this paper, the authors proposed a real-time, language
and vocabulary independent, multi-view accounting and
speaker-independent speech reconstruction system

entries.text: The view-classifier evaluation does not state the train/test split, sample counts, speaker overlap, or a chance-level baseline; uniform guessing across five balanced classes would be 20% (inference).
entries.condition: Five-way view classification; the paper states balanced classes and an overall accuracy but not the test protocol.

entries.text: Across the reported model evaluations, no random seeds, independent repeated training runs, or run-level uncertainty intervals are specified; the ten OOV iterations are phrase leave-outs, not reported seed repeats.
entries.condition: Applies to classifier, reconstruction PESQ results, text-prediction accuracy, delays, and user-study summary unless stated otherwise; no seed information appears in the paper.
entries.quote:
We use 60 epochs for training and 20 epochs for ﬁne-
tuning the network.

entries.text: The paper does not identify the exact speaker-dependent phrase subset or phrase identities used for the two-train/one-test split, nor report phrase-wise or speaker-wise repeated evaluations.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent single-view and view-combination PESQ experiments; the text describes three phrases per speaker for this protocol, while the database section describes ten phrases.

entries.text: The paper does not describe a separate validation/selection set for choosing the best view combination; it says the speaker-independent setup uses the combination selected from earlier experiments.
entries.condition: View-combination selection precedes speaker-independent and OOV reporting; whether selection uses a distinct validation set is not stated.
entries.quote:
For speaker independent settings, the best view combina-
tion as obtained from the experiments above was taken.

entries.text: Text-prediction Config-1 does not state whether the random sample split keeps speaker identities disjoint; its description partitions audios from all speakers, so speaker overlap across partitions is possible.
entries.condition: Text-classification accuracy 97.0%; contrast with Config-2, which explicitly partitions by speakers.

entries.text: No visual pixel normalization, audio feature normalization, or normalization of predicted LPC/LSP values is reported.
entries.condition: Reconstruction inputs and outputs; the paper reports image dimensions, audio sampling rate, LPC order, and LSP encoding only.

entries.text: The paper does not report statistical tests, confidence intervals, or uncertainty across independent training runs for the PESQ, accuracy, or delay comparisons.
entries.condition: Tables 1–12 report point values/means and limited user-study variance summaries only.
entries.quote: Table 4: Mean readings for single-view PESQ scores for Lipper and (Ephrat and Peleg 2017)

entries.text: The single-view Vid2Speech baseline's exact dataset split, speaker/phrase test condition, and whether its PESQ values were recomputed on the same test set are not stated.
entries.condition: Table 4 compares target-model scores with values attributed to Ephrat and Peleg (2017).
entries.quote:
We have compared our results with
(Ephrat and Peleg 2017) which train a similar speech-
reconstruction network and tested it on single-view visual
feed.

entries.text: Delay measurement hardware and timing boundaries are not stated, and the paper does not say whether the compared systems were timed under the same conditions.

The comparison of delay values is
reported in Table 11.

entries.text: User-study participant demographics, total judgments, item sampling, answer-order randomization, blinding, and the definition/calculation of the reported variance are not described.
entries.condition: Audio-only and audio-visual phrase identification studies; audio-only reports 10 annotators and 25 speakers, while the second-study count is not separately specified.

entries.text: The paper does not specify which original audio/reference recordings were paired with reconstructed speech for PESQ, beyond describing PESQ's two-audio alignment and comparison procedure.
entries.condition: All PESQ tables; expected reference is not explicitly identified in the evaluation description.

entries.text: No external language model, lexicon, or linguistic rescoring step is described for reconstructing or decoding speech; the described output decoder maps the network's encoded audio to sound.
entries.condition: Language/vocabulary-independence claim; a separate text-prediction classifier does map encoded audio to predefined phrase categories for analysis.

questions.q: What evidence supports the paper's claim that multi-view input improves reconstructed speech, and which view combination is best?
questions.answer: The speaker-dependent PESQ tables show 0°+45°+60° at 2.315, the best reported multi-view value (t47); this is higher than all-view PESQ 2.086 (t64). The authors also report 0°+45° as the best two-view setup (t33, t42), but comparisons are point estimates without reported uncertainty (t104).

questions.q: Does the evaluation establish generalization to unseen speakers and unseen phrases equally well?
questions.answer: No. OOV evaluation holds out phrases while keeping each speaker represented in training; its reported phrase PESQ values range from 1.46 to 1.84 (t19, t66–t75). Speaker-independent testing holds out two speakers, but the authors report a weaker result and acknowledge this as a deployment limitation (t18, t77–t80).

questions.q: How strong is the evidence that reconstructed audio is intelligible?
questions.answer: The user studies report 80.25% audio-only accuracy and 81.25% audio-visual accuracy, against stated chance levels of 25% and 10% respectively (t87–t91, t125–t126). The study protocol and variance computation are only partially specified (t108), and the authors caution that PESQ itself can misrepresent perceived quality (t92).

questions.q: Do the delay and language-independence claims demonstrate deployment readiness?
questions.answer: The paper reports 0.169 s Lipper delay per phrase and qualitative demos in Hindi, English, and Chinese (t82–t86, t114–t119, t94), but it does not report matched timing hardware/protocol or quantitative language-held-out evaluation (t107, t94). It also states the system is limited to controlled, stable-camera conditions (t96).

questions.q: For Vid2speech (arxiv-1701.00495), improved Vid2speech (arxiv-1708.01204) and Lip2AudSpec (arxiv-1710.09798): objective intelligibility metric, listener test design (open transcription vs forced choice), unseen speakers?
questions.answer: Reader run (oc_run.sh) stopped on a usage limit; writer grepped the specific passages. Vid2speech: listeners classify each word among GRID vocabulary options, 23 MTurk workers (p29, p11). Lip2AudSpec: transcription plus 1-5 naturalness, 20 workers per sample (p30, p31, p12). Improved Vid2speech: STOI and ESTOI plus PESQ and ViSQOL (p32).
